blocks.text: Propositional equivalence is a concept in propositional logic. It explains when two logical expressions have the same meaning. Even if expressions look different, they may give the same result. Propositional equivalence is checked using truth tables. If two expressions have the same truth values in all cases, they are equivalent. The symbol “≡” is used to show equivalence. Propositional equivalence improves clarity in reasoning (as shown in Figure 2.6).

blocks.alt: A box stating that two propositional expressions are logically equivalent: Expression 1, (A AND NOT B) OR (B AND NOT A), and Expression 2, (A OR B) AND (NOT A OR NOT B), joined by a double arrow; both are true in the same cases (XOR). A Venn diagram shades A only and B only, leaving the overlap and the outside unshaded, with a four-part key. A truth table and a closing line Therefore: Expression 1 is equivalent to Expression 2.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.6: Two logically equivalent propositional expressions, by Venn diagram and truth table (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.6).
blocks.long_description: Key: A AND NOT B; B AND NOT A; Neither A nor B; A AND B (not included). Truth table rows (A, B, Expression 1, Expression 2): F F F F; F T T T; T F T T; T T F F.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Equivalent expressions may look different but always give the same result; they help simplify complex logic.

Equivalent logical expressions are identified using truth tables. Each expression is tested for all possible truth values. If the results match in every case, they are equivalent. Logical laws can also help identify equivalence. These laws simplify expressions. Identifying equivalence helps reduce complex expressions.

Equivalence is important because it helps simplify logic problems. It allows us to replace complex expressions with simpler ones. This saves time and effort. In programming, equivalent expressions improve code efficiency. Equivalence helps avoid logical errors. It ensures correct reasoning and decisions. This concept is useful in mathematics and computer science. Understanding equivalence strengthens logical thinking.
